Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s informal labour market is attracting digital platforms seeking to connect independent workers with households and businesses, as technology companies explore ways to organise a services economy largely driven by personal referrals and informal networks.
3H Jobs, a Nigerian digital hiring platform launched in Lagos on November 20, is seeking to tap into this market by connecting artisans, general workers, and other service providers with individuals and businesses. The company is targeting at least 300,000 workers on its platform by the end of January 2027. About 93 percent of employed Nigerians were in informal employment in the second quarter of 2024, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), highlighting the scale of a labour market where many workers operate outside conventional employment structures.
For artisans, technicians, drivers, and other independent service providers, securing jobs often depends on personal contacts, while households and businesses face challenges verifying skills, finding reliable workers, and resolving disputes over service delivery. This creates an opportunity for digital marketplaces to reduce the cost of finding service providers and give independent workers access to a wider customer base. However, turning that opportunity into a sustainable business will depend on generating regular transactions, retaining customers, and keeping payments within their platforms. 3H Jobs covers services ranging from plumbing, electrical repairs, and construction to cleaning, driving, hospitality, fashion and entertainment. “Some artisans are highly skilled, and some are simply willing to work, but they have no way for the right person to find them,” said Olabisi Olayemi, speaking on behalf of the founder of 3H Jobs, at the platform’s launch.
To build trust between customers and service providers, the company said it would use manual verification, professional certification checks where applicable, and customer ratings. It also operates an escrow-style payment arrangement under which customers fund jobs before work begins, with payments released after confirmation that the agreed service has been completed.
The arrangement is intended to reduce disputes over poor workmanship and non-payment. However, keeping transactions within the platform could prove difficult. Company representatives acknowledged that 3H Jobs currently has no binding arrangement preventing customers and artisans from taking subsequent transactions outside its system. “We presently don’t have that kind of binding law,” a company representative said in response to a question about how it would prevent service providers from bypassing the platform after securing customers.
The company said it could only take responsibility for transactions conducted within its system. This presents a commercial risk for digital marketplaces because customers and workers who establish relationships through a platform may subsequently transact directly, reducing the volume of business processed through the platform and limiting its ability to earn revenue from completed jobs. 3H Jobs did not disclose its revenue model, the number of workers currently registered or the investment required to achieve its 300,000-worker target.
Registration is currently free for both customers and service providers, with applicants able to list multiple services under one account. The company also plans to work with training institutions, corporate organisations and development partners to equip underprivileged Nigerians with practical skills and connect them to potential customers. For digital platforms targeting the informal labour market, the opportunity extends beyond registering thousands of workers. Their commercial prospects will ultimately depend on converting those registrations into completed jobs, repeat customers and transactions that generate sustainable revenue.
Ayomide Odunlami is a Tax Reporter at BusinessDay, covering Nigeria’s tax reforms, compliance trends, and government revenue strategies. She reports on how evolving tax policies affect businesses, investors, and the broader economy, providing clarity on complex regulatory issues through data-driven journalism.
